doc.title: Wendy Oxenhorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 22, 2026

title: Unpaid royalties and the cheating of musicians
summary: Asked about recovering owed royalties, she describes unfair contracts, publishing denied, and flat session fees with no royalties.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Did you ever get involved in trying to recover, and this is a legal avenue sort of, trying to recover owed payments or royalties for things that they had written that they had been cheated out of? Was that part of what you ended up doing?

It’s funny you should put it that way but there was really not much recourse. There were contracts they signed with labels, record companies, for their own publishing that they could never get. I remember a musician telling me a very famous label, when he said that he wanted his own publishing the executive said to him, “No,” – and I’m not going to use the N word – but he said, “No N is going to ever have his own publishing while I’m alive.” You know? This is how it was when you recorded with someone like Frank Sinatra, you know, the horn section. You got three hundred dollars for the gig, for the recording, and then there were no royalties on the vinyl that was sold. There was nothing else. So you got to pay your rent once. And then CDs were invented, there was nothing in contracts, CDs weren’t invented yet. There was nothing to cover people. It would have been wonderful if there was a class action suit that could do something like that but I don’t think there was anyone interested and if they were I do know there were record labels would often try to buy out attorneys, just like in divorces you hear of this. You know? The rich husband goes to the lawyer the wife is using and does something to make it a conflict of interest for him to be able to represent her. You know I think there had to be payoffs, things like that. I’m not going to assume but you know it wasn’t done, so what I would tell the musicians when they had a hard time accepting help from the Jazz Foundation was think of this as all the money that you never got that you should have when you were cheated by clubs that didn’t pay properly or promoters that took advantage of you when you were on the road, all the hotels that should have been covered for you while you were touring, the food that should have been covered for you, you know and you come back almost breaking even from a European tour. That they were able to absolutely assimilate and say okay, that I can do.
